title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the mass, the ranking and the bare infinitive

questions.prompt: Complete both gaps in this line from an association's yearly report: "We thank the large ___ of parents who gave up their Saturdays, and we apologize for the small ___ of equipment we were able to offer them."

options.text: amount ... number
number ... number
amount ... amount
number ... amount

questions.explanation: "number ... amount" is the pair the two nouns call for: parents are people you can count one by one, and a countable plural takes a number of, while equipment is uncountable and can only be measured, an amount of. "amount ... number" reverses both and produces the two mistakes at once. "number ... number" counts a mass, which is what a large number of equipment tries to do and no English sentence does. And "amount ... amount" measures people as if they were a substance, which the first gap refuses.

questions.prompt: Emna's school has exactly two libraries: the old one in the main building and the new one beside the yard. The new one is bigger. Emna wants to say so in a single sentence for the school magazine. Which line is correct?

options.text: The new library is the biggest of the two.
The new library is the most big of the two.
The new library is bigger than the old one.
The new library is more bigger than the old one.

questions.explanation: "The new library is bigger than the old one." is the correct line: only two libraries are being compared, and a difference between two is the work of the comparative, bigger, followed by than. "The new library is the biggest of the two." reaches for the superlative, which English keeps for three or more; between two, it would say the bigger of the two. "The new library is the most big of the two." makes the same error and adds a second one, since a one-syllable adjective builds its forms with -er and -est, never with most. And "The new library is more bigger than the old one." marks the comparison twice, once with more and once with the ending, where one mark is enough.

questions.prompt: Complete this sentence from an account of the campaign: "Before the bell, the head teacher had two senior pupils ___ the posters in every corridor."

options.text: to put up
put up
putting up
puts up

questions.explanation: "put up" is the form: after have somebody, exactly as after make somebody and let somebody, the second verb is a bare infinitive, an infinitive with no to. "to put up" keeps the to that these three verbs refuse, which is the single most frequent mistake of the whole point; it is the form allow would take, allowed them to put up. "putting up" is an -ing form, and the frame the lesson gives, have somebody do something, asks for an infinitive and not for a form in -ing. And "puts up" adds a third person -s, although the only conjugated verb in the sentence is had; the second verb never carries a tense of its own here.

questions.prompt: Hedi is testing the noun "homework" against the six lines of the rule, one line at a time. Which of these four statements about it is true?

options.text: It becomes homeworks when there are several exercises.
It can be preceded by one, as in one homework.
It takes many in front of it, as in many homework.
It takes a singular verb, whatever the amount of it.

questions.explanation: "It takes a singular verb, whatever the amount of it." is the true statement: an uncountable noun has one form and one agreement, so the verb stays singular however much work has been set, as in The homework is difficult tonight. "It becomes homeworks when there are several exercises." gives a plural to a noun that has none; the number of exercises changes nothing, because the noun names the mass and not the items. "It can be preceded by one, as in one homework." fails the very test that defines an uncountable noun, since no cardinal number can stand in front of it. And "It takes many in front of it, as in many homework." borrows the modifier of countable plurals; homework takes much.

questions.prompt: A pupil's account of the first day of the anti-violence week reads: "Nobody was asked, and nobody was given the choice of staying outside. At eight o'clock the whole school was sitting in the hall." Complete the line that reports what the head teacher did: "The head teacher ___ the opening talk."

options.text: let every class attend
allowed every class attend
made every class attend
had every class to attend

questions.explanation: "made every class attend" is what the account describes: nobody was asked and nobody could stay away, which is obligation, and obligation is the value of make somebody do something, with the second verb in the bare infinitive, attend. "let every class attend" is built correctly and says the opposite: let grants a choice, and the account states in so many words that no choice was given. "had every class to attend" misses twice: have somebody do something arranges a task with the people whose part of the work it is, which a whole school is not, and it never puts to in front of the second verb. And "allowed every class attend" misses twice as well, since allow carries the same permission as let, so the meaning is wrong, and allow is the one verb of the four that does need to, allowed every class to attend.

questions.prompt:
Read this table from a school report on the anti-violence week, then answer. "Pupils who took part, by year group.
First year: 140 in 2023, 155 in 2024, 168 in 2025.
Second year: 210 in 2023, 196 in 2024, 174 in 2025.
Third year: 90 in 2023, na in 2024, 121 in 2025." (na means not available.) Which conclusion do these figures support?

options.text: Taking part fell in the second year group and rose in the first.
The third year group took part less in 2024 than in 2023.
The first year group was the largest group of the school in 2025.
Fewer pupils took part in 2025 than in 2023 in every group.

questions.explanation: "Taking part fell in the second year group and rose in the first." is the conclusion the table supports: read across, the second year group goes 210, 196, 174, which is a steady fall, and the first year group goes 140, 155, 168, which is a steady rise. "The third year group took part less in 2024 than in 2023." reads a figure into a cell marked na: not available means nothing at all can be said about that year, neither more nor less. "The first year group was the largest group of the school in 2025." confuses the pupils who took part with the pupils there are: the table counts volunteers, never the size of a year group. And "Fewer pupils took part in 2025 than in 2023 in every group." is contradicted by two rows out of three, since the first group rose from 140 to 168 and the third from 90 to 121.
